title: Design YouTube (Video Streaming)
summary: End-to-end walkthrough: resumable uploads, a parallel transcoding DAG, HLS/DASH adaptive bitrate via CDN, and view counts aggregated off the hot path.
body:
## Practice first

Design a video platform where creators upload videos and viewers watch them on phones, laptops and TVs with smooth playback, even on poor networks. Each video shows a title, description and a view count.

Spend about 10 minutes sketching first: requirements, entities, upload and watch endpoints, a baseline diagram, and the two or three deep dives you would choose. Then read on and compare. The reasoning is the point; product names are interchangeable.

## Functional requirements

Core (users should be able to):

1. **Upload a video** (up to, say, 256 GB / several hours) with title and description.
2. **Watch a video** with playback that adapts to device and bandwidth.
3. **See video metadata and view counts**, and find videos by searching titles.

Out of scope: recommendations and the home feed, comments, live streaming, monetization and ads, copyright matching (mention it as a pipeline stage only), and creator analytics dashboards.

## Non-functional requirements

- **Scale:** about 1 billion daily active viewers watching ~5 billion videos/day; roughly 500 hours of video uploaded per minute.
- **Playback latency:** time to first frame under ~2 s and minimal rebuffering at p99. This drives everything about delivery: the bytes must come from a CDN near the viewer.
- **Availability vs consistency, per operation:** watching favours availability (99.99%); metadata edits and view counts can be eventually consistent (seconds to minutes). Upload acceptance must be durable: once we say "upload complete", the original must never be lost.
- **Processing latency:** a typical 10-minute video should be watchable within a few minutes of upload; longer videos can take longer, but progress should be visible.
- **Cost:** storage and egress dominate; the design should avoid storing or serving renditions nobody watches.

## Back-of-the-envelope

- **Egress:** 5B views/day × ~10 minutes watched × ~2.5 Mbps average ≈ 5e9 × 600 s × 2.5e6 bit / 8 ≈ 9.4e17 bytes/day ≈ 940 PB/day, or ~87 Tbps average. No origin can serve this. Decision: **CDN delivery is mandatory**, and hit ratio matters more than origin throughput.
- **Upload ingest:** 500 h/min of 1080p source at ~8 Mbps ≈ 500 × 3,600 s × 1 MB/s ≈ 1.8 TB/min ≈ 30 GB/s. Decision: **direct-to-blob resumable uploads**, never through API servers.
- **Transcoding compute:** if one CPU core encodes one rendition at about real time and we produce ~6 renditions in 2 codecs, that is 500 h/min × 60 × 12 ≈ 360,000 core-hours per hour of wall clock, i.e. ~360,000 cores busy continuously. Decision: **split videos into segments and transcode them in parallel on a large worker fleet**; per-video latency then depends on segment length, not video length.
- **View counts:** 5B views/day ≈ 58,000/s average, with single viral videos taking tens of thousands/s. Decision: **never increment a row per view**; aggregate in a stream.
- **Metadata:** ~1B videos × ~5 KB ≈ 5 TB; reads are huge but cacheable. A sharded store keyed by `video_id` with a cache is enough.

## Core entities

- **Video:** id, creator, title, description, status (`uploading`, `processing`, `ready`, `failed`), duration, visibility.
- **Upload:** id, video id, object-store key of the original, parts received.
- **Rendition:** video id, codec, resolution, bitrate, manifest location.
- **Segment:** a few seconds of one rendition; immutable object in blob storage.
- **TranscodeJob:** video id, stage, segment range, status, attempts.
- **ViewCount:** video id, aggregated count (approximate, eventually consistent).

## API

```http
POST /v1/videos
Authorization: Bearer <token>
{ "title": "Rebuilding a carburetor", "description": "...", "sizeBytes": 4294967296, "contentType": "video/mp4" }

201 Created
{ "videoId": "v_8f2", "uploadId": "up_31", "partSize": 16777216,
  "partUrls": [ { "part": 1, "putUrl": "https://blob.example.com/...signed..." } ] }
```

```http
POST /v1/videos/{videoId}/upload/complete
{ "uploadId": "up_31", "parts": [ { "part": 1, "etag": "\"a1b...\"" } ] }
202 Accepted  { "status": "processing" }
```

```http
GET /v1/videos/{videoId}
200 OK { "videoId": "v_8f2", "title": "...", "status": "ready", "views": 10342,
         "manifestUrl": "https://cdn.example.com/v_8f2/master.m3u8" }

GET /v1/search?q=carburetor&cursor=...
200 OK { "results": [ ... ], "nextCursor": "..." }

POST /v1/videos/{videoId}/views
{ "sessionId": "s_1", "watchedSeconds": 31 }
204 No Content
```

Uploads and metadata edits require auth; watching public videos does not. Part URLs are presigned, short-lived and can be re-requested for any missing part, which is how resume works. Search uses cursor pagination.

## High-level design

**Requirement 1, upload.** The Video service creates a `Video` row in `uploading` state and starts a multipart upload in the object store, returning presigned part URLs. The client uploads parts in parallel and retries failed parts. On `complete`, the object store assembles the original, the video moves to `processing`, and an event goes onto the processing queue.

**Requirement 2, watch.** A pipeline transcodes the original into several renditions (for example 240p to 2160p), each cut into 2–6 second segments with HLS/DASH manifests, and writes them to blob storage. The player fetches the master manifest from the CDN, picks a rendition, then fetches segments, switching renditions as measured bandwidth changes.

**Requirement 3, metadata, search and views.** Metadata lives in a sharded database behind a cache. Changes flow via change-data-capture into a search index. Players send view beacons into a stream; aggregators update counts.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CR["Creator client"] --> API["Video service"]
    CR -->|"multipart PUT"| RAW[("Blob: originals")]
    API --> MDB[("Metadata DB")]
    RAW -->|"upload complete"| Q[["Processing queue"]]
    Q --> TP["Transcode pipeline"]
    TP --> SEG[("Blob: segments and manifests")]
    TP -->|"status ready"| MDB
    SEG --> CDN["CDN edge"]
    V["Viewer player"] --> CDN
    V --> API
    V -->|"view beacons"| VS[["View event stream"]]
    VS --> AGG["Count aggregator"]
    AGG --> MDB
    MDB -->|"CDC"| SI[("Search index")]
```

Walk a watch request: the viewer opens a video page; the Video service returns metadata from cache, including the CDN URL of `master.m3u8`. The player downloads the master manifest (a list of renditions), chooses 720p based on screen size and a bandwidth estimate, downloads the 720p media playlist, then fetches segments one after another from the nearest edge. If throughput drops, the next segment is requested from the 480p playlist instead. Every 30 seconds or so, the player sends a view beacon.

## Deep dives

### 1. The transcoding pipeline (processing latency and cost)

**Bad: one worker transcodes the whole video into all renditions sequentially.** A 3-hour video at real-time speed across 12 outputs takes a day and a half; a worker crash restarts everything.

**Good: one job per rendition, in parallel.** Better, but the longest rendition still runs as long as the video, and a crash loses hours of progress.

**Great: a DAG of small jobs over segments.** Split the original at keyframes into ~10-second chunks. Each `(chunk, rendition)` pair is an independent, idempotent task whose output is keyed deterministically (for example `v_8f2/720p/seg_00042.ts`), so retries overwrite rather than duplicate. Fan-in steps assemble manifests and generate thumbnails; a parallel branch runs content checks. A workflow orchestrator (or a job table plus queue) tracks the DAG, retries failed tasks with backoff, and marks the video `ready` when the required renditions finish.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    O[("Original")] --> SPLIT["Split at keyframes"]
    SPLIT --> T1["Encode chunks: 360p"]
    SPLIT --> T2["Encode chunks: 720p"]
    SPLIT --> T3["Encode chunks: 1080p"]
    O --> AUD["Extract and encode audio"]
    O --> CHK["Safety and copyright checks"]
    O --> THB["Thumbnails"]
    T1 --> MAN["Write HLS and DASH manifests"]
    T2 --> MAN
    T3 --> MAN
    AUD --> MAN
    MAN --> READY["Mark video ready"]
    CHK --> READY
    THB --> READY
```

Splitting first makes every encode task small and parallel; the manifest step waits for all chunk tasks, and publication waits for checks. Two cost levers: publish as soon as low and medium renditions are done (higher ones appear later), and only produce expensive codecs (AV1) or 4K for videos that become popular. Workers are stateless and can run on preemptible capacity because tasks are short and idempotent.

### 2. Adaptive bitrate streaming (playback latency)

**Bad: serve one MP4 file with progressive download.** A phone on 3G either stalls on a 1080p file or gets a 240p file on fibre. Seeking far ahead needs range requests and still cannot change quality.

**Good: several MP4s at different qualities, chosen once at start.** Better first choice, but quality cannot adapt when the network changes mid-video.

**Great: HLS or DASH.** Each rendition is a sequence of short segments, all aligned on the same timestamps, described by a media playlist; a master manifest lists the renditions. The player measures download throughput and buffer level and chooses the rendition for each next segment. Segments are plain HTTP objects, so any CDN caches them. Segment duration is a trade-off: 2-second segments adapt faster and start quicker; 6-second segments mean fewer requests and better compression. Using CMAF lets one set of fMP4 segments serve both HLS and DASH, halving storage.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Player
    participant E as CDN edge
    participant S as Segment origin
    P->>E: GET master manifest
    E-->>P: renditions 360p..1080p
    P->>E: GET 720p playlist
    E-->>P: segment list
    P->>E: GET 720p seg 1
    E->>S: cache miss, fetch
    S-->>E: segment
    E-->>P: segment (now cached)
    P->>P: throughput drops, buffer low
    P->>E: GET 480p seg 2
    E-->>P: segment (cache hit)
```

The player, not the server, decides quality, which keeps the origin stateless. Popular segments stay hot at the edge; only the first viewer in a region pays for the origin fetch.

### 3. CDN delivery and the long tail (latency and cost)

Most views go to a small fraction of videos, but the catalogue is enormous. Popular videos sit in edge caches with near-100% hit ratio. Long-tail videos miss at the edge; use a tiered cache (edge → regional shield → origin) so one regional fetch serves many edges and the origin sees mostly unique requests. Manifests are tiny and can have short TTLs; segments are immutable and can be cached for a very long time with versioned URLs. Pre-warm edges for videos expected to spike (a scheduled premiere). Signed URLs or tokens protect private and unlisted videos without making segments uncacheable: sign at the playlist level, or use cookie-based CDN authorization.

### 4. Resumable uploads (durability of the original)

Multi-gigabyte uploads from home connections must survive drops and laptop sleeps. Use the object store's multipart upload: fixed parts (16–64 MB), each uploaded with a presigned URL and retried independently; the client persists `uploadId` and completed parts locally. On resume, it asks the server (which can list uploaded parts) what is missing. The original is only acknowledged once `complete` succeeds and the object exists durably, at which point processing starts. Abandoned multipart uploads are cleaned up by a lifecycle rule after a few days. Keep the original indefinitely: codecs improve, and re-encoding from the source beats re-encoding from a lossy rendition.

### 5. View counts at scale (throughput vs freshness)

**Bad: `UPDATE videos SET views = views + 1` per view.** A viral video makes one row the hottest lock in the database at tens of thousands of writes per second.

**Good: sharded counters.** Spread increments over N sub-rows and sum on read. It removes the single hot row but still costs a database write per view.

**Great: stream aggregation.** Players send beacons to a log such as Kafka partitioned by `video_id`. A stream processor deduplicates by session, applies validity rules (minimum watch time, bot filtering), and every few seconds writes aggregated deltas (`+3,412`) to the count store. Displayed counts lag by seconds to minutes, which the product accepts. Store a separate, slower "audited" count if counts drive payments. Hot keys in the stream can be pre-aggregated in the producer or partitioned by `(video_id, random salt)` and merged.

### 6. Metadata and search (read scale)

Metadata is read-heavy and keyed by `video_id`: shard by it and front it with a cache, since a video page is the same for everyone. Search goes to an inverted index (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) populated from the metadata DB via change-data-capture, so the database stays the source of truth and the index can be rebuilt. Index only `ready`, public videos; a short indexing lag is acceptable.

## What interviewers look for

- **Mid-level:** separate upload, processing and playback paths; blob storage plus a CDN; asynchronous transcoding; a metadata DB distinct from video bytes.
- **Senior:** chunked, parallel transcoding as a DAG with idempotent tasks; a clear explanation of HLS/DASH manifests and segments and why the client chooses bitrate; resumable multipart uploads; view counting that avoids hot rows.
- **Staff:** cost as a first-class requirement (on-demand high renditions, codec choices, tiered caching, egress), handling of failure and partial publication, multi-region origins, abuse and content safety stages, and how operational signals (rebuffer ratio, time to first frame, processing latency) steer the design.

## Common mistakes

- Serving video bytes from application servers or the origin bucket without a CDN.
- Describing "transcoding" as one opaque step with no parallelism or retry story.
- Confusing a manifest with a segment, or having the server pick the bitrate.
- Incrementing a view counter row on every play.
- Making the upload acknowledge before the original is durably stored.
- Indexing search directly from application code instead of from a durable change stream.

## Self-review checklist

- [ ] Upload bytes go directly to blob storage in resumable parts.
- [ ] Transcoding is split into idempotent tasks with a clear DAG and retry policy.
- [ ] You can draw the master manifest → playlist → segment hierarchy.
- [ ] Segments are immutable and cached at the edge with long TTLs.
- [ ] View counts are aggregated asynchronously with a stated freshness.
- [ ] Every estimate you quoted changed a decision (CDN, parallel encode, stream counts).
- [ ] Video status transitions (`uploading` → `processing` → `ready`/`failed`) are durable.

## Further reading

- [RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8216)
- [Netflix Technology Blog](https://netflixtechblog.com/)
- [Amazon S3: Multipart upload overview](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html)
keyTakeaways: Egress of hundreds of petabytes a day makes CDN delivery of immutable segments the core of the design, not an optimisation.
Transcode as a DAG of small idempotent tasks over keyframe-aligned chunks so per-video latency does not scale with video length.
Adaptive bitrate works because each rendition is aligned short segments listed in manifests and the player chooses quality per segment.
Large uploads use multipart presigned parts that retry and resume independently; the original is kept for future re-encodes.
View counts are aggregated from a partitioned event stream, trading seconds of staleness for no hot-row writes.
